name: SCAMPER
use_case: An offer, service, product or routine already exists and does its job, but it has gone stale and people have stopped seeing how it could be different. The team wants a steady stream of concrete ideas for changing it, working from the thing as it is today and questioning it piece by piece, rather than inventing something new from a blank page.
strengths: starts from something that already exists, so nobody faces an empty page and every idea is anchored in a real offer or process
seven fixed prompts push thinking in directions people would not take on their own, such as dropping a part entirely or reversing the order of steps
can be used by one person at a desk as well as by a group in a workshop, with no materials beyond a list of the prompts
quick to learn; in one expert study a fifteen-minute introduction was enough for participants to use it
works on services and administrative processes as well as on physical products
the prompt that produced each idea is recorded, which makes it easy to see which kinds of change have and have not been considered
weaknesses: yields variations of what exists; it rarely leads to a fundamentally different kind of answer
produces many ideas of very uneven quality and does not help choose between them; a separate evaluation step is always needed
some prompts fit a given object badly, and groups waste time forcing answers under every letter
assumes the problem is already understood; it cannot tell whether the existing offer is the right thing to improve at all
the research evidence is thin: a handful of design studies, mostly small and short, rather than a body of controlled trials
in a group it inherits the usual problems of spoken idea rounds, such as dominant voices and early criticism, unless the session is structured
use_cases: Our school has run the same introduction day for new teachers for years; it covers what it should, but newcomers find it dull, and the team wants ideas for reworking it that start from the programme we already have.

A teacher has taught the same course unit the same way for a long time and wants to rethink it lesson by lesson, asking for each part what could be swapped, merged, left out or done the other way round.

A public library's lending and events offer is used steadily but no longer attracts new visitors, and staff want to produce variants of the existing services instead of designing a new programme from nothing.
A company sells a well-established product and wants a set of variants and spin-offs derived from the current design, by changing its materials, size, uses or the order of its parts one at a time.
audience: individuals working on their own offer
